content:
Although Apple has long made privacy a selling point of its hardware and services, I sometimes wonder whether Apple regrets rolling out one privacy measure: App Tracking Transparency (ATT).

Such a relatively limited feature somehow feels like almost every month it faces a new antitrust lawsuit or regulatory challenge. The UK is now seeing its third ATT lawsuit—and this one has a special twist.

This article has been updated at the end with Apple's response…

The personalised advertising debate

Personalised advertising has been a hot topic in the tech world for years. Instead of seeing random ads for products we may or may not be interested in, we are shown ads based on interest profiles collected from the apps we use and the websites we visit.

In theory, this is a win-win for everyone. Consumers see ads they may genuinely be interested in; advertisers get better ad performance thanks to precise targeting; and free apps and websites that rely on ad revenue earn more for the same reason.

Although the data used to deliver personalised ads is collected anonymously, the practice has led many to view it as a privacy invasion. Even though Apple has developed a technology specifically to ensure the anonymity of such data, many consumers remain sceptical.

App Tracking Transparency

Apple's App Tracking Transparency is designed to address this by giving consumers the choice over whether their data can be used to deliver personalised ads. Developers wishing to collect such data must obtain consumer consent first.

Unfortunately for the iPhone maker, this move has triggered a string of lawsuits and antitrust investigations, with the main point of contention being that Apple's own apps do not ask for this consent. Apple has repeatedly pointed out that its rules are actually consistent: Apple's own apps do not show the ATT prompt because they do not collect the data that the prompt covers. Third-party apps that do not collect such data are also exempt and do not need to show the prompt.

The latest UK lawsuit

Apple has so far faced three complaints at the UK's relevant antitrust regulator—the Competition Appeal Tribunal. Apple lost the first case—though it is currently appealing—and the second case is still ongoing.

Reuters reported on the third case, filed today.

The special twist

The latest lawsuit has an interesting angle: it was brought by Ann Pope, who was once a senior official at the regulator involved in this case.

Ann Pope, a former senior official at the UK's Competition and Markets Authority who is now leading this lawsuit, said Apple's policies "have caused very serious harm to businesses that depend on Apple as a gatekeeper." Pope stated in a declaration: "This action is vital to protecting the rights of UK businesses that depend on Apple, to ensure that the rules Apple implements are fair, and to obtain compensation for the losses suffered by UK businesses."

After a recent investigation by Germany's antitrust regulator, Apple agreed to make eight changes to its ATT rules across the EU. Regarding this lawsuit, the company responded to us as follows:

Over the years, multiple privacy advocates have publicly voiced their support for ATT.
